title: Zohran Mamdani makes surprise appearance on CNN’s ‘Have I Got News for You’ | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

“Have I Got News for You” airs Saturdays at 9 p.m. ET on CNN and is available to stream the following day for CNN’s All Access subscribers and on HBO Max.

“We’re gonna have someone fun come out,” Roy Wood Jr. told the studio audience for CNN’s comedy panel show “Have I Got News for You” on Friday afternoon.

Judging by the cheers and applause, the audience was happily surprised by what happened next.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined Wood on stage for a jovial conversation about politics, including the Senate leadership race and the mayor’s much-scrutinized relationship with President Donald Trump.

The episode, which will air Saturday at 9 p.m. Eastern on CNN, demonstrated the in-demand mayor’s unconventional approach to media appearances

While he hasn’t appeared on “Saturday Night Live,” he dropped by “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” when Kimmel was in Brooklyn last September, and made a cameo on “The Tonight Show” soon after his inauguration in January.

“This is crazy. I was actually here to see John Oliver,” Mamdani joked during the CNN taping, knowing that Oliver’s HBO show is taped in the same building on the far west side of Manhattan.

The timing of Friday’s “Have I Got News for You” visit was notable for a couple of reasons. First, it was one of Mamdani’s first interviews since the Democratic Party retook control of Congress in the midterm elections; second, it was slightly complicated by the fact that Mamdani is on crutches right now.

On Thursday evening, the mayor sustained an injury during a soccer game with members of the New York City press corps. “I tore my Achilles,” he told reporters at a press conference Friday morning.

“Have I Got News for You” producers worried that he might cancel, but Mamdani still participated in the taping, seated at the table with his crutches kept off-screen.

“I got scared when you showed up, because usually when you show up in New York, it’s to fix something,” Wood said, making a joke about his own job security.

Then Wood and his panelists pretended to continue with the show as planned, beginning with the question, “Can Mamdani pull off this mustache?”

The mayor explained that he is participating in “Movember” to raise awareness about men’s health issues.

Panelist Amber Ruffin sounded smitten. “You’re Homecoming king right now,” she quipped. “And maybe, always?”

The comedians offered theories about Trump’s unexpectedly cordial working relationship with Mamdani.

“It’s like, you know that old Life cereal commercial? ‘Mikey hates everything, but he likes Life.’ I feel like that’s Trump with you,” panelist Michael Ian Black said.

Mamdani posited that “the one thing we do have in common is this city,” given Trump is a native New Yorker; whenever they talk, the mayor said, “I try and focus our conversations around housing, how to build more housing.”

Mamdani let the professionals crack most of the jokes. When the show turned to Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who recently urged Trump to embrace Medicare for All as “Trumpcare,” Black remarked, “If Trump goes for El-Sayed’s pitch, and he’s a fan of yours, is there any chance we could convert him to Islam?”

Mamdani laughed, smiled and waited a beat while thinking about what to say.

“It’s never come up in our conversations,” he responded.

Mamdani also weighed in on Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s challenge against Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Schumer declined to endorse Mamdani for mayor last year, and Mamdani hasn’t backed Schumer in the majority leader contest.

Black asked him: “Do you have a preference?”

“I think less about who it should be and more about what they should do,” Mamdani said, arguing that “the point of power is to use it, to deliver.”

Mamdani stayed on message and avoided direct criticism of Schumer. Later in the conversation, he said, “I don’t think grudges are worth holding, because grudges don’t pay people’s bills. And to me, I think that our politics has to be, how do we help New Yorkers pay their bills?”
